vc_tomography · how a scan type is calibrated and reconstructed

BM18 helical pair: calibration and filtered backprojection

Two helical scans of one sample, with the rotation stage moved sideways between them so that together they cover a field wider than the detector. This page follows one such acquisition, PHerc0343P at 8.64 µm on ESRF BM18, from its raw frames to a reconstructed slice: what the geometry and intensity calibrations measure, and how the default reconstruction, filtered backprojection, uses them.

The acquisitionCommandsGeometry calibrationIntensity calibrationFiltered backprojectionThe sliceWhat is measured but not applied

The acquisition

A helical pair is two scans of one sample. In each the sample turns continuously while the stage carries it along the rotation axis, so every part of the sample crosses the detector's rows over several turns. Between the two scans only the stage under the rotation moves across the beam (yrot): the rotation axis falls on another detector column, and the sample stays where it was on the rotation stage. The first scan (HA) has the axis inside its field; the second (TA) has it at the detector's edge and records the field beside HA's. Together they cover a field about twice the detector's width.

Commands

The pipeline has three steps, in a fixed order: the geometry calibration, the intensity calibration (which lays out the merged frame from the geometry), and the reconstruction. These are the commands of docs/calibration.md and docs/reconstruction.md for this scan type, as they were run for this page.

vc_tomography_calibration geometry  HA.h5 TA.h5 --out CAL/geometry.json
vc_tomography_calibration intensity HA.h5 TA.h5 --geometry CAL/geometry.json --out CAL
vc_tomography_reconstruct PROJ --cache_dir CAL --fractions 0.5 --tag fbp_default

No option beyond the defaults is needed. vc_tomography_reconstruct PROJ alone also works: it runs both calibrations on first use and caches them.

Geometry calibration

To put a raw pixel value on the line through the sample that it measured, the reconstruction must know, for every frame of every scan, which ray each detector pixel recorded. The geometry calibration measures this from the scans' own frames and writes it to one file, geometry.json.

The model

A ray through the sample is named by the angle θ it is seen at, its distance s from the sample's origin across the beam (pixels) and its height z (rows). A stored pixel (c, v) looks along the ideal position (X, Y) = (c + Eu, v + Ev), where Eu(c, v) and Ev(c, v) are the detector map (lens distortion). Scan k records the ray at

X = axisk + axis_slopek·(H − Hmid,k) + A(2θ) + u + roll·(Y − middle row)
Y = z + heightk + (1 + axial_scalek)·H + B(θ) − roll·u
u = s + dk·(cos θ, sin θ)

θ and H are the angle and height that the master records, taken at the time the pixel's row was exposed: row v of frame f at the time of frame f + row_time·(v − middle row). The unknowns are:

  • axis, axis_slope: the rotation axis' column in the scan, and its drift per row of travel along the axis;
  • axial_scale: the sample really travels (1 + axial_scale) rows per row of recorded travel (the helical pitch);
  • height, d: the scan's height and the sample's place on the rotation stage, against the first scan (the anchor, where both are zero);
  • roll: the rotation of the detector's columns against the rotation axis;
  • A, B: what the rotation stage does within a turn, shared by all scans: the axis column twice per turn and the sample's height once per turn;
  • Eu, Ev: the detector map, a polynomial of the third order in the pixel's position;
  • tilt: a small tilt of the sample between scans, solved in a second pass with the axial scales held.

The solve of this acquisition has 33 free unknowns for 9 858 patch matches. Everything is solved together as one least-squares problem (Ceres), with a Huber loss of 0.03 px on each match so that a wrong match cannot pull the solution. No match has an offset of its own: what the model cannot explain stays in the residuals.

Layout

The step first reads what it can without registering anything precisely: the frames on disk, the frames per turn, the rows that hold something across the whole width (the sample mount, kept out of every comparison), the direction of the detector's rows against the stage's travel, and a coarse rotation axis per scan. A scan with the axis in its field gets the axis from profiles of frames half a turn apart; a scan without it is placed against its neighbour by profiles at equal frames.

Row time

The detectors read their rows one after another while the sample turns (a rolling shutter), so each row of a frame belongs to a slightly different angle, and in a helix to a slightly different height. The calibration needs the time between two rows.

Here it is measured from a refill of the storage ring that fell inside HA's helix. Each injection shot dims the beam for about a millisecond. A row integrates for 30 ms of every 33 ms frame, starting later (or earlier) the further down it lies, so a shot dims some rows in one frame and the rest in the next. Where that split falls, shot after shot, depends on the row time alone. The step takes the level of every row in the columns that hold air (columns 8 to 444), finds the shots and fits all of them at once: -19.874 ± 0.083 µs per row from 94 shots on a raster of 249.99 ms. Over the 1200 rows that is -0.72 of a frame period; the sign says the last row is read first.

Comparisons

Fine measurements come from registering blocks of frames that recorded the same lines through the sample on different parts of the detector. A block is 32 frames by up to 512 columns; it is cut into patches of 128 × 128 stored pixels, and each patch is registered to a fraction of a pixel in frames, rows and columns (band-passed phase correlation, repeated until no displacement is left). A patch is accepted with a correlation above 0.3.

  • Opposite views: a stretch against itself half a turn on, mirrored about the coarse axis column. They exist only where the axis lies inside the field, in the strip of columns that is seen from both sides. 2 951 patches.
  • One turn apart: the helix against itself a turn on, in the rows that both turns hold. 268 patches.
  • Rest turn against helix: a turn at rest against the helix turn nearest its height, at equal angle. 2 235 patches.
  • Scan against scan: two scans at equal angle, across the columns (or rows) both hold. 4 404 patches.

Solve

The detector map is free in full here (15 terms). The pair determines it because its comparisons span the detector: the largest correlation of a map term with another unknown is 0.92, below the 0.95 at which the step would hold the term.

Intensity calibration

The intensity calibration turns raw counts into transmission and decides how much each scan contributes where scans overlap. It computes, per scan:

  • Dark: the mean of the dark frames.
  • Flats: the mean of each flat series, every flat frame first scaled to the nominal ring current of 0.2 A (dark + (flat − dark)·0.2 / I), as the ESRF reference workflow reduces them.
  • Weight map: the mean flat over its maximum, smoothed by a Gaussian of 10 px, times a taper at the top and bottom rows. Bright, well-lit pixels count more.
  • Apodisation: a taper across the columns at every edge that overlaps another scan, and for the first scan a slope across the rotation axis, so that the scans cross-fade instead of meeting at a step.
  • Placement: where each scan lies in the merged frame, from the geometry calibration's poses (the median axis column and row offset over the frames, rounded to a quarter pixel; the exact pose of every projection stays in its own terms).
  • Detector blur field: how the detector's sharpness varies over its area, fitted to the noise spectra of 200 flats on tiles of 128 px. It is used by sharpness_weighting=auto.

For this pair the merged frame is 3 372 columns wide with the rotation axis at column 2528.25. TA lies at (rows, columns) = (+1.00, -843.50) from HA. The blur field is kept: it explains the flats' noise spectra (residual 0.453 → 0.348) and reaches 2.8 px along the columns at the worst corner, with none at column 1 194.

Filtered backprojection

The default method is filtered backprojection (backprojector=fbp) with no projection filter. It reconstructs a chunk of slices in the stages below; every stage has a CPU and a CUDA implementation with the same results. All scans are gridded into one sinogram per slice in the merged frame, so the volume is reconstructed once, not per scan.

  1. Read. For each scan, the projections that see the chunk's slices and, of each, only the detector rows the slices fall on, plus the context rows of the kernels.
  2. Flat-field. Each raw sample becomes a transmission: (raw − dark) / (flat − dark), with the flat interpolated between the series and the projection scaled by its ring current.
  3. Grid. Each projection is read at the pose the geometry calibration gives it. Along the axis, the slice lies at a fractional detector row, read with a 16-row Lanczos kernel (z_interp=lanczos8) through the detector map's row displacement. Across the beam, each row is resampled exactly (a band-limited, non-uniform Fourier resampling, x_interp=sinc) onto the ideal columns at the scan's fractional offset. The value times its weight, and the weight, are added into the sinogram row of the projection's angle.
  4. Match brightness. Each scan after the first is matched to the scans before it in a 25 × 25 px window at their seam (luminosity_repartition).
  5. Divide and mend. The sums are divided by the summed weights, which gives the weighted mean transmission of every ray. Columns without weight take the nearest measured value.
  6. Filter, then −log. Projection filters (Paganin phase retrieval, unsharp mask, ...) act here; the default chain is empty. Then the transmission becomes a line integral, −ln, clipped to [10⁻⁶, 10].
  7. Balance. A line through the sample may be recorded twice, from opposite sides. Each recording gets the weight W / (W + W of the opposite view, mirrored about the axis), so that every line counts once.
  8. Ramp filter. Each sinogram row is filtered with the Ram-Lak ramp (filter_name=ramlak). The row is padded with its opposite view, mirrored about the axis, so the filter does not see a cut where a scan's field ends.
  9. Backproject. Each filtered row, times its balanced weight, is smeared back across the slice along its rays: the backprojector is exact and pixel-driven, the rows upsampled twice (FFT) and interpolated with a cubic B-spline (fbp(interp=bspline3, oversample=2)). Values are scaled to linear attenuation in cm⁻¹.

Details that depend on the calibration:

  • One sinogram row per view (angle_interp=views). The sinogram of this slice has 9 290 rows on an angular grid of 8 000 bins per turn: a slice is seen for more than one turn where the detector is taller than the travel per turn, and two views a turn apart are not at exactly the same angle. Each is filtered and backprojected at its own measured angle with its share of the weight.
  • Row time. A slice lies on another detector row in every projection, so the angle of each sinogram row is corrected per slice by the row time (−0.72 of a frame period from the first row to the last).
  • Beam divergence. The BM18 source is far away: the rays turn by 49 nrad per stored column, which the backprojector follows in the slice.
  • Sharpness weighting (sharpness_weighting=auto). Where a ray is recorded twice, the spatial frequencies above 0.15 to 0.30 cycles per pixel are taken more from the recording made where the detector is sharper, by the blur field. Below that band the usual weights apply.

The slice

What is measured but not applied

  • Slices are reconstructed one at a time in a two-dimensional model. Anything that moves a ray out of its slice is not applied: the beam's divergence along the axis, and a tilt of the rotation axis towards the beam.
  • Of a scan's tilt against the first, the part about the beam's direction is applied (as a turn of each frame); the part about the direction across the beam and a spin about the axis are not. The file manifest.json of every run lists them under provenance.geometry.measured_not_applied.
